title: Interrupted pendulum

caveats: central support pole briefly occludes the string and ball
string catches on middle clamp so pendulum length changes mid-swing
thin string may blur during fast swing

slow_motion.evidence: no narration, captions or on-screen text about slow motion; motion appears real-time

observation.what_happens: A yellow ball on a string is held out to the right and then released. It swings down through the middle and up to the left, with the string catching on a middle peg to shorten the pendulum, then swings back and forth.

calibration.note: yellow tennis ball = 0.067 m (given with the clip) spans 51 px in SAM's mask

given: scale: yellow tennis ball = 0.067 m (given with the clip) spans 51 px in SAM's mask
pendulum length L = 0.497 m, measured from the radius of the swing with the ruler: hold L fixed and measure g
reasoning: Path fits a 0.497 m circle over an 84 deg arc with theta from +0.77 to -0.70 rad, so it is a large-angle pendulum with given L. Zero crossing at ~1.4 s is much slower than 1-g, implying slow-motion apparent g, with slight decay and asymmetric timing from the peg shortening the left side. Candidates therefore test small vs large angle, viscous damping, and a two-length peg model with speed-conserving catch/release.

critique.finding: The ball swings like an ideal pendulum with pull of {g} on a string of length {L}. It misses the late swings, so no candidate law really captured the motion.
critique.headline: Ball swings simply at first then peg changes rhythm
critique.revision_idea: Add a peg that shortens the string on one side, making a two-length pendulum. Early bins fit well but the last bin pulls strongly one way, just as a sudden shortening would cause.
critique.why_it_won: It keeps full swing height with wide arcs while the damped version adds unneeded friction.

headline: Ball swings simply at first then peg changes rhythm
finding: The ball swings like an ideal pendulum with pull of 0.551 ± 0.0013 m/s² on a string of length 0.497 m. It misses the late swings, so no candidate law really captured the motion. That is 18× weaker than Earth’s gravity, so the clip most likely plays about 4.2× slower than real life.

eyeball.confidence: medium-low, roughly 60% - length scale from ball/hand and timing from real-time video each ~15-20% uncertain
eyeball.law_in_words: Interrupted/Galileo pendulum: T = 2*pi*sqrt(L/g). Right side swings with L_long = pivot to ball ~1.0-1.2 m from tennis-ball scale, left side swings with L_short = peg/clamp to ball. Time release to bottom is T_long/4, bottom to left peak is T_short/4, full return is (T_long+T_short)/2 ~1.6-1.8 s in real-time video. Solving g = 4*pi^2*L_long/T_long^2 gives ~9-10 m/s^2, consistent with ball returning to same dashed-line height showing energy conservation.

clock.note: Gravity came out 18× too weak. Either this happened somewhere with 0.056× Earth's gravity, or the clip plays about 4.2× slower than real life (slow motion). Run it again with the slow-motion factor set.
